title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
subject: Science
chapter: 1. Exploring the Investigative World of Science
description: Practice on how scientists investigate — focused questions, controlling variables, fair tests and careful observation — plus the Grade 8 Curiosity roadmap from microbes to climate.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is the purpose of the questions on the first page of each chapter?
options: To spark curiosity about the world
To test reading speed of students
To prepare students for the exam
questions.explanation: Page 1 says these questions 'are not meant for any exam — they are unique invitations to spark your curiosity to explore the world of science'.

questions.question: The 'Probe and ponder' questions are meant to be answered in the annual exam.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter states clearly that these questions are not meant for any exam; they are invitations to be curious.

questions.question: One Probe-and-ponder question compares the number of grains of sand on all beaches and deserts with the number of —
options: drops of water in the oceans
questions.explanation: The question asks whether there are more grains of sand on all the beaches and deserts of the world, or more stars in our galaxy.

questions.question: The diversity question on page 1 says we have been observing the variety of plants and animals 'right from' which grade?
questions.explanation: The text says 'Right from Grade 6, we've observed the incredible diversity of plants and animals around us.'

questions.question: Which of these questions actually appear in the chapter's 'Probe and ponder' box? (Select all that apply)
options: Why is one side of a puri thinner than the other?
Why has nature created such a vast variety of living things?
Why does the Moon appear reddish during an eclipse?
Why do magnets attract iron but not wood?
questions.explanation: The box asks about the thin side of a puri, sand grains versus stars, and why nature created such a vast variety. Eclipses and magnets are not in the box.

questions.question: The chapter invites you to write your own curious question on page 1. What does this tell you about how the book views the reader?
options: As an examiner who grades answers
As a reader who only follows the text
As a learner who memorises given facts
As an investigator who asks questions
questions.explanation: The book addresses you as 'Young Scientists' and wants you to be investigators who ask your own questions, not just memorise facts.

questions.question: What is the name of the NCERT Grade 8 science textbook this chapter belongs to?
questions.explanation: The running header reads 'Curiosity — Textbook of Science for Grade 8', and the text says 'Our journey with Curiosity ... continues in Grade 8'.

questions.question: In Grade 6, according to the chapter, science began with —
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls that in Grade 6 'science begins with wonder, with simple Why? and How? questions about the world around us'.

questions.question: Which idea was the focus of Grade 7, as recalled in this chapter?
options: Science is a fixed collection of facts proven long ago
Science is mainly about naming and classifying living things
Science is always evolving and each answer opens new questions
Science needs a laboratory and precise measuring instruments
questions.explanation: In Grade 7 we learnt that science is always evolving, each answer opens new questions, and our ideas slowly change as we explore deeper.

questions.question: Grade 8 is described as the 'Investigative World of Science' where which two things come together?
questions.explanation: The chapter says that in Grade 8 'wonder and evolution come together to form the heart of how science works' — wonder from Grade 6 and evolution from Grade 7.

questions.question: The chapter says 'we don't want you to just learn new facts.' What does it want instead?
options: To learn how to find new facts
To learn many more facts faster
To learn facts from older books
To learn facts only from teachers
questions.explanation: The exact line is: 'we want you to learn how to find new facts' — the skill of investigation, not just more facts.

questions.question: According to the chapter, investigation in science means simply looking at something and asking simple questions.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter says investigation 'means more than just looking at something and asking only simple questions' — it needs focused questions and experiments.

questions.question: Which of these are listed in the chapter as part of investigating like a young scientist? (Select all that apply)
options: Copying results from a reference book
questions.explanation: Investigation means asking focused questions, designing simple experiments to answer them, and using observations to improve understanding. Memorising or copying is not investigation.

questions.question: The chapter gives two example puzzles: 'why does dough rise?' and 'is the world getting warmer?'. What contrast do they illustrate?
questions.explanation: The puzzles 'may range from everyday life — like why does dough rise? — to the bigger mysteries of Earth and beyond like is the world getting warmer?'

questions.question: Put the chapter's steps in order: using questions as starting points, we then try to —
options: explain what we expect, then observe, then conclude
explain clearly, then observe, then experiment
observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully, explain clearly
experiment first, then ask the question, then explain
questions.explanation: The chapter's order is: use questions as starting points, observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully, and explain clearly what we see.

questions.question: Where on the page is the image of a root printed?
questions.explanation: On the left-hand pages, at the bottom, you find the image of a root; the kite is in the top corner of the right-hand pages.

questions.question: What does the kite symbol in the book stand for?
questions.explanation: The kite soaring in the sky reminds us 'that curiosity must take flight if we are to explore the unknown'. The root stands for rooted knowledge.

questions.question: The root symbolises a foundation of knowledge that keeps us connected to —
questions.explanation: The root symbolises 'the deep, solid foundation of knowledge that keeps us connected to our environment, traditions, and our cultural and natural heritage'.

questions.question: The chapter says investigation works best when careful observation is balanced with creative thinking.
questions.explanation: True. 'Investigation in science works best only when we balance the solid ground of careful observation with the freedom of creative thinking.'

questions.question: A student only daydreams about wild ideas and never checks them against observations. In the chapter's symbols, which part is missing?
options: The page numbers of the textbook
The root — grounding in real observation
The lines at the bottom of the page
questions.explanation: The root stands for staying 'grounded in real observations'. Wild ideas without observation have the kite but lack the root.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the patterns in the lines at the bottom of each page?
options: They show the page number in a secret code
They are decorations copied from Grade 7
They mark the end of each topic clearly
They hide scientific thoughts and reduce boredom
questions.explanation: There are 'some hidden scientific thoughts' in these patterns, but 'they are mainly to make the page a little less boring'.

questions.question: In the textbook, the kite appears in the top corner of the right-hand pages.
questions.explanation: True. The kite is in the top corner of right-hand pages; the root is at the bottom of left-hand pages.

questions.question: Which pairing of symbol and meaning is NOT correct according to the chapter?
options: Kite — ideas soaring to new horizons
Root — deep, solid foundation of knowledge
questions.explanation: Freedom of creative thinking belongs to the kite, not the root. The root is the solid ground of careful observation and knowledge.

questions.question: The journey this year begins by examining something as small as —
questions.explanation: 'We will start by examining something as small as a single drop of water, and uncover a hidden world of tiny organisms.'

questions.question: Which of these is given as a role of 'invisible helper' microbes?
questions.explanation: Some microbes are invisible helpers 'that help us digest our food or produce medicines'. Infections are caused by the harmful ones; UV shielding is the atmosphere's job.

questions.question: Which of these does the chapter list as helping us stay healthy and fight infections? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter lists nutritious food, exercise, medicines and vaccines. Sunlight and cold drinks are not mentioned.

questions.question: According to the chapter, all microbes are harmful and cause infections.
questions.explanation: False. Some microbes are 'invisible helpers' that aid digestion or produce medicines; only some are harmful and cause infections.

questions.question: Microbes are described as 'unseen but deeply linked to us'. Which statement best captures this link?
options: They live only outside the human body
They are linked to us through sunlight
They are seen only through a telescope
They can both help us and harm us
questions.explanation: The link is two-sided: helpers aid digestion and make medicines, while harmful ones cause infections. Telescopes view distant objects, not microbes.

questions.question: Besides digestion, what other helpful job of microbes is mentioned?
questions.explanation: The helpers 'help us digest our food or produce medicines'. The other jobs, though real elsewhere, are not mentioned in this chapter.

questions.question: Medicines and vaccines are mentioned in the chapter as ways to —
questions.explanation: 'We'll find out how nutritious food, exercise, medicines, and vaccines help us stay healthy and fight infections.'

questions.question: Which effect of electric current is said to keep us warm?
questions.explanation: 'We depend on the heating effect of electric current to keep us warm, while the magnetic effect helps motors run.'

questions.question: Which effect of electric current helps motors run?
questions.explanation: The magnetic effect of electric current 'helps motors run and machines function'; the heating effect keeps us warm.

questions.question: Why does the chapter move from electricity to the study of forces?
options: Because electrical phenomena depend on fundamental forces
Because forces were skipped in Grades 6 and 7
Because motors and heaters do not need electricity
Because forces are easier to measure than current
questions.explanation: 'These phenomena depend on fundamental forces. So after watching electricity do work, we move on to study these forces themselves.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, forces can make objects — (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Forces 'make objects speed up, slow down, or change direction'. Colour and lightness are not effects of force mentioned in the chapter.

questions.question: A ball thrown up in the air falls back to the ground. The chapter uses this to illustrate —
options: the heating effect of electric current
the magnetic effect of electric current
how light bends when passing through air
questions.explanation: 'Understanding forces helps explain why a ball thrown up in the air falls back to the ground, or why a car stops when the brakes are applied.'

questions.question: Which everyday example in the chapter shows a force making an object slow down?
options: A motor turning when switched on
A ball thrown up falling back down
A car stopping when brakes are applied
A puri puffing up in boiling hot oil
questions.explanation: Brakes apply a force that slows and stops the car. The falling ball shows a force changing motion downward, and the motor shows the magnetic effect of current.

questions.question: The chapter says the magnetic effect of electric current is what keeps us warm.
questions.explanation: False. It is the heating effect that keeps us warm; the magnetic effect helps motors run.

questions.question: Which statement about forces is NOT supported by the chapter?
options: Forces help explain why brakes stop a car
Forces can change an object's direction
Forces can make a moving object slow down
Forces act only on objects that are moving
questions.explanation: The chapter never restricts forces to moving objects; it says forces make objects speed up, slow down or change direction. The other three statements are from the text.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe pressure?
options: How force is distributed over an object
The total weight of the atmosphere above
The energy carried by fast-moving wind
The speed at which air moves around us
questions.explanation: The chapter introduces 'the idea of pressure — how the force is distributed over an object'.

questions.question: According to the chapter, a small difference in pressure results in —
questions.explanation: 'A small difference in pressure can result in a gentle breeze while a stronger pressure difference can lead to strong winds, and sometimes even cyclones.'

questions.question: What can a stronger pressure difference lead to, according to the chapter?
options: Morning fog and sometimes heavy dew
questions.explanation: A stronger pressure difference 'can lead to strong winds, and sometimes even cyclones'. Rain, earthquakes and fog are not linked to pressure difference here.

questions.question: The chapter states that the same concepts of force and pressure decide how air moves.
questions.explanation: True. 'The same concepts of force and pressure also decide how air moves.'

questions.question: The chapter says powerful weather events like storms and cyclones affect which of the following? (Select all that apply)
options: The distance of Earth from the Sun
questions.explanation: Storms and cyclones 'affect our daily lives, agriculture, and even our safety'. Moon phases and Earth's distance from the Sun are astronomical and unaffected.

questions.question: Imagine two neighbouring regions with almost equal air pressure. Based on the chapter, what would you predict?
options: Strong winds will blow from both sides
The air will become very hot and rise
A cyclone will form between them
Only a gentle breeze, if any, will blow
questions.explanation: Wind strength depends on pressure difference: a small difference gives at most a gentle breeze; cyclones need a strong pressure difference.

questions.question: To understand how air exerts pressure, the chapter says we need to —
options: zoom in and study the particles it is made of
study the phases of the Moon carefully
observe storms and cyclones from far
measure wind speed with special instruments
questions.explanation: 'To truly understand how air can exert pressure ... we need to zoom into these materials and see what kind of particles they are made up of, and how they move around.'

questions.question: In which type of material can particles move around freely, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: 'In materials that are solid these particles cannot move much, while in gases they can move around freely.'

questions.question: How are particles in a solid described?
options: They do not exist in solids
questions.explanation: In solids the particles 'cannot move much'; it is in gases that they move around freely. Everything, including solids, is made of particles.

questions.question: Which of these is described as a 'pure substance'?
questions.explanation: The chapter classifies materials into 'elements (pure substances), compounds (two or more elements bonded together), and mixtures'.

questions.question: How does the chapter define a compound?
options: Two or more elements bonded together
A pure substance that cannot be broken down
A solid in which particles cannot move
A combination that can be separated physically
questions.explanation: A compound is 'two or more elements bonded together'. Physically separable combinations are mixtures; 'pure substance' is the label for elements.

questions.question: What is the key feature of a mixture given in the chapter?
options: Its parts can be separated physically
It is always a single pure substance
It is always a liquid solution
questions.explanation: Mixtures are 'combinations that can be separated physically'. Bonding describes compounds, and purity describes elements.

questions.question: Sugar dissolving in tea to make it sweet is the chapter's example of —
questions.explanation: 'We can then understand solutions — for example, how sugar dissolves in tea to make it sweet.' Dissolving does not bond sugar into a compound.

questions.question: According to the chapter, classifying things around us is an important feature of science.
questions.explanation: True. 'Classifying things around us is an important feature of science', e.g. sorting materials into elements, compounds and mixtures.

questions.question: Which statement about materials is NOT correct according to the chapter?
options: Elements are classed as pure substances
Everything around us is made of tiny particles
Particles in gases can move around freely
questions.explanation: It is mixtures that can be separated physically; compounds are elements bonded together. The other three statements are straight from the chapter.

questions.question: Which pairs correctly match a category with its description from the chapter? (Select all that apply)
options: Compound — two or more elements bonded
questions.explanation: Elements are pure substances and compounds are two or more elements bonded together. Mixtures (not compounds) can be separated physically; bonding is not a feature of mixtures.

questions.question: The chapter says we need to zoom into materials and their particles to explain why water boils at a certain temperature.
questions.explanation: True. To understand 'why water boils at a certain temperature we need to zoom into these materials and see what kind of particles they are made up of'.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what happens to light when it passes through a lens?
questions.explanation: Light 'bends when passing through lenses'; it reflects off mirrors.

questions.question: Light is said to reflect off which kinds of mirrors in this year's study?
questions.explanation: 'We'll study how light rays reflect off flat and curved mirrors, and bends when passing through lenses.'

questions.question: How does the chapter explain the way corrective glasses help us see clearly?
options: Through the heating effect of light
questions.explanation: 'The bending of light explains ... how corrective glasses help many of us see clearly.' Glasses are lenses, and lenses bend light.

questions.question: According to the chapter, only polished mirrors can reflect light.
questions.explanation: False. 'It's not just a polished mirror that reflects light, rough surfaces reflect light as well, and so does the Moon.'

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as something that reflects light?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists polished mirrors, rough surfaces and the Moon as reflectors. A lens is described as bending light, not reflecting it.

questions.question: Seeing an image in a shiny metal spoon is mentioned alongside which topic?
options: The light chapter on mirrors and lenses
The chapter on forces and pressure
The chapter on particles and mixtures
questions.explanation: The spoon image is given while describing the study of light — reflection from curved surfaces and bending through lenses.

questions.question: Which objects does the chapter mention when discussing reflection and bending of light? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions the image in a shiny metal spoon and corrective glasses. Torches and prisms are not mentioned.

questions.question: What causes a slightly different part of the Moon to be lit each night?
options: The Moon producing light of its own
Relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun
Clouds covering parts of the Moon
The Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
questions.explanation: 'Depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is illuminated each night, giving rise to the phases.'

questions.question: Watching the periodic cycles of the Moon's phases allowed humans to come up with —
questions.explanation: 'Watching the periodic cycles of the Moon's phases allowed humans to come up with the first calendars.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, various calendars came into being by combining observations of —
questions.explanation: 'By combining careful observations of sunrises, sunsets, and lunar cycles, various calendars came into being.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, the Moon reflects light rather than producing its own light.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter lists the Moon among things that reflect light, along with polished mirrors and rough surfaces.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call it 'fascinating' that calendars determine our routines?
options: Because they depend on motions of objects far beyond Earth
Because every country on Earth follows the same calendar
Because the Moon directly controls the weather on Earth
Because calendars were only invented in the last century
questions.explanation: 'Isn't it fascinating that the calendars which determine our routines on Earth are linked to the motions of objects far beyond our planet?'

questions.question: The calendar page shown in the chapter is for the month of Chaitra. Which dates does it cover?
questions.explanation: The calendar image is labelled 'Chaitra (March 22 - April 20, 2025)'.

questions.question: On page 7 the chapter mentions 'the shrinking bright part of the Moon after purnima'. What must the Moon look like on purnima?
questions.explanation: The bright part can only shrink after reaching its largest, so purnima is the night the Moon is fully lit (full Moon). After it, the lit part decreases night by night.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the phases of the Moon are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter attributes phases to the relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun, which change how much of the lit Moon we see — not to Earth's shadow.

questions.question: Living beings depend on and respond to air, water, sunlight and other organisms, forming —
questions.explanation: Every living being 'depends on and responds to the air, water, sunlight, and other organisms around them forming the ecosystems that support life on our planet'.

questions.question: Which reason does the chapter give for water remaining liquid on Earth?
options: Earth's perfect distance from the Sun
questions.explanation: 'The Earth lies at the perfect distance from the Sun, where water remains liquid.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, Earth's atmosphere does which of the following? (Select all that apply)
options: Shields us from harmful ultraviolet rays
Produces light for the phases of the Moon
questions.explanation: The atmosphere 'provides the oxygen we breathe while shielding us from harmful ultraviolet rays'. It does not stop evaporation or light the Moon.

questions.question: The chapter's phrases 'from tiniest insect to the largest whale' and 'from blades of grasses to tall trees' are used to emphasise that —
options: only large organisms matter in ecosystems
every living being depends on its environment
plants and animals live in separate places
insects and whales share the same food
questions.explanation: The phrases stress that every living being, small or large, depends on and responds to air, water, sunlight and other organisms.

questions.question: The final chapter of the book tries to understand what makes Earth 'just right' for life.
questions.explanation: True. 'In the final chapter of this book, we can put it all together and try to understand what makes Earth just right for life.'

questions.question: The relationships between living organisms and their environments are described in the chapter as —
questions.explanation: The chapter speaks of 'marvellous and complex patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments'.

questions.question: If Earth were much farther from the Sun, which chapter statement would be most directly affected?
questions.explanation: Water stays liquid because Earth is at the perfect distance from the Sun; move Earth away and that condition changes. The other statements do not depend on distance from the Sun.

questions.question: According to the chapter, who lies 'at the heart of both the problem and any possible solution' for Earth's climate?
questions.explanation: 'At the heart of both the problem — and any possible solution — is us. We are the ones influencing Earth's climate.'

questions.question: What does the chapter say human activities can do to Earth's temperature?
options: Cause changes only in the polar regions
Cause small changes that disrupt climate patterns
Cause no measurable change to climate patterns
Cause large changes that are quickly reversed
questions.explanation: 'Human activities on the planet can cause small changes in the temperature of the Earth, disrupting climate patterns, with dangerous consequences.'

questions.question: Which scientific principles does the chapter say will be key to protecting the balance on which life depends? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: 'The same scientific principles ... observing, measuring, experimenting — will be key in helping us protect the delicate balance on which life depends.'

questions.question: The chapter claims that the challenges facing the planet will always be easy to solve with science.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter says 'the challenges ahead won't always be easy', while hoping students will try to solve them with Curiosity as a guide.

questions.question: The chapter says small changes in Earth's temperature can have 'dangerous consequences'. Which chain of cause and effect matches the text?
options: Changed temperature → human activities → disrupted climate
Human activities → disrupted climate patterns → changed temperature
Human activities → changed temperature → disrupted climate patterns
Disrupted climate → human activities → changed temperature
questions.explanation: The text: human activities cause small changes in temperature, which disrupt climate patterns, which have dangerous consequences.

questions.question: What does the chapter hope some students will do with 'Curiosity as your guide'?
options: Score the highest marks in science
Build a laboratory at their homes
Write a new textbook for Grade 9
Try to solve difficult planetary problems
questions.explanation: 'We hope some of you will try to solve these difficult problems with Curiosity as your guide.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, we are the ones influencing Earth's climate, but we are also the ones who can use science to guide our actions.
questions.explanation: True. 'We are the ones influencing Earth's climate. But we are also the ones who can — and must — use science to understand these changes and guide our actions.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, where can simple science experiments be done without a fancy laboratory?
questions.explanation: 'You don't need a fancy laboratory to do simple experiments. Even your kitchen at home is a wonderful place to observe and ask questions.'

questions.question: Which question does the chapter say starts a kitchen investigation?
questions.explanation: 'All you need is to start with curiosity, careful observation, and asking what happens if…?'

questions.question: Which of these are things the chapter says we can CHANGE or CONTROL in the puri experiment? (Select all that apply)
options: Time taken for the puri to puff
Whether the puri puffs up or not
questions.explanation: Thickness, size, flour type, oil temperature and dropping method are things we control. Puffing (yes/no) and time to puff are things we observe or measure.

questions.question: In the puri experiment, 'the time it takes to puff up (seconds)' is an example of —
questions.explanation: The chapter separates what we can change from what we can observe or measure; time to puff up, in seconds, is a measured observation.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a way of dropping the dough into the oil?
questions.explanation: The chapter suggests dropping the dough 'vertically', sliding it 'at an angle', or sliding it 'slowly'. Pricking a hole is a separate later question.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as something we can change in the puri experiment?
questions.explanation: Oil temperature, dough size and thickness, flour type and dropping method are all listed. The pan's colour is not mentioned.

questions.question: The chapter mentions that a phulka puffs up when placed in hot oil.
questions.explanation: False. A puri or batura puffs up in hot oil; the phulka 'swells when put directly on the flame'.

questions.question: The chapter says observations in the puri experiment may be of two kinds. Which pair is correct?
options: Colours and smells noted in words
questions.explanation: 'Some of these may have just yes/no answers, in some cases there might be a number we can measure.'

questions.question: A student wants to check 'whether a very thick layer of dough still gives a thin side'. What type of result is this?
questions.explanation: Whether a thin side forms is a yes/no observation. The thickness of dough is the controlled variable; the result is what we observe.

questions.question: While doing an experiment, the chapter advises changing —
options: only one thing at a time
questions.explanation: 'It is better to change only one thing at a time while keeping the other conditions same.'

questions.question: To compare boiling hot, hot and not-very-hot oil fairly, what must be kept the same?
options: Dough thickness and way of dropping
Type of oil and size of the pan
Number of puris and their colour
Time of day and room temperature
questions.explanation: The chapter's example: to test oil temperature 'we would use circles of dough of the same thickness, and drop them in the same way'.

questions.question: A student fries a thick puri in very hot oil and a thin puri in warm oil, then concludes that hot oil puffs puris better. What is wrong?
options: The puri should have been pricked first
Two things were changed at the same time
Oil temperature should never be changed
The student should have used maida flour
questions.explanation: Thickness and temperature both changed, so the difference cannot be blamed on temperature alone. Change only one thing at a time.

questions.question: Why does the chapter recommend keeping notes of everything you see and sense?
options: To avoid having to repeat the experiment again
To prove the experiment was done in the kitchen
To make sense of the changes and think of new questions
To fill the notebook before the teacher checks it
questions.explanation: Notes of what you see and sense help make sense of changes, and 'after doing one round of experiments, you may think of more questions'.

questions.question: Which observations does the chapter suggest noting about the oil? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: 'Did the oil splatter, smell, or smoke?' are the sensory observations suggested. Brand and price are not observations of the experiment.

questions.question: After one round of experiments, which NEW question does the chapter suggest?
options: Does the colour of the plate change the taste?
Does the size of the stove affect the oil?
Does the brand of flour change its price?
Do puris puff better from fresh or stored dough?
questions.explanation: The follow-up questions are: 'Do puris puff better when made fresh or from stored dough? What happens if I prick a hole in the puri before frying?'

questions.question: The chapter suggests testing what happens if a hole is pricked in the puri before frying.
questions.explanation: True. One follow-up question is 'What happens if I prick a hole in the puri before frying?'

questions.question: Changing only one thing at a time while keeping other conditions the same is important because —
options: it shows which change caused the difference
it uses much less flour and oil overall
it is a rule required by every textbook
it makes the experiment finish faster
questions.explanation: The chapter says we change one thing at a time 'to make sense of the changes' — only then can a difference be linked to the one thing changed.

questions.question: The chapter calls the step-by-step way of doing experiments —
questions.explanation: 'This is exactly how all scientific experiments ... are done. This is the idea of systematic investigation.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, the puffing of a puri is now completely understood by scientists.
questions.explanation: False. 'Even this simple everyday observation — of a puri puffing — is not really completely understood by scientists today!'

questions.question: What does the chapter say about how complicated scientific experiments are done compared with simple ones?
options: They need no questions to begin with
They are done only by professionals
They follow the same systematic approach
They skip the observation step entirely
questions.explanation: 'This is exactly how all scientific experiments, from simple to the most complicated are done' — by systematic investigation.

questions.question: Which statement about the puri investigation is NOT supported by the chapter?
options: New questions arise after a first round of experiments
The same method applies to complicated experiments
Even everyday observations can be investigated scientifically
Scientists have fully explained why puris puff up
questions.explanation: The chapter says puri puffing is 'not really completely understood by scientists today'. The other three statements are made in the text.

questions.question: The chapter ends by comparing the puffing of a puri with —
options: the shrinking bright part of the Moon
the boiling of water in a kettle
the swelling of a phulka on a flame
the slow rising of fresh bread dough
questions.explanation: 'Whether it is the puffing of a puri or the shrinking bright part of the Moon after purnima, let your careful observations guide you.'

questions.question: Which of these are part of the chapter's idea of systematic investigation? (Select all that apply)
options: Changing one condition at a time
Keeping notes of what you see and sense
Accepting the first result as final
questions.explanation: Systematic investigation changes one thing at a time and records everything observed; one round of experiments leads to more questions, not a final verdict.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by saying 'let your careful observations guide you'?
options: Observations should be kept secret from others
Observations should decide what you explore next
Observations should be replaced by guesses
Observations matter only in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Observations are the 'solid ground' that guide explorations and lead to new questions — in the kitchen as much as in a laboratory.

questions.question: The chapter signs off with the words 'Happy experimenting!'
questions.explanation: False. The last line of the chapter is 'Happy investigating!'
